query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, phase stability is governed by a balance between strong local chemical clustering driven primarily by attractive Al–Ni (and Al–Al) interactions and the stabilizing effect of configurational entropy. At lower Al levels (e.g., Al mole fraction ~0.1), the high configurational entropy dominates, preserving a single-phase FCC structure that delivers optimal high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness. In contrast, increasing the Al content above a critical threshold (e.g., >0.3) enhances local clustering, promotes the emergence of dual-phase (FCC+BCC) or multiphase microstructures, and thereby degrades these targeted properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys synthesized with a controlled, equimolar base composition and varied only in Al content (for example, comparing an alloy with Al mole fraction 0.1 vs one with Al mole fraction 0.5). The alloys are processed to achieve a homogeneous single-phase solid solution initially.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the Al mole fraction (e.g., x = 0.1 versus x = 0.5) and subject the alloys to isothermal annealing at temperatures spanning from ambient to high temperatures (e.g., up to 1000 °C) and apply controlled compressive loading (and/or ion irradiation) as needed to trigger the clustering-to-ordering transition.
generation.conditions: Annealing at selected temperatures (e.g., 500 °C, 700 °C, 1000 °C) under inert atmosphere to preclude oxidation; mechanical loading tests (compression/tensile) at room and cryogenic temperatures; and, where applicable, controlled ion irradiation to simulate displacement damage.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of short-range ordering measured by the pair correlation functions (e.g., Al–Al and Al–Ni pair probabilities) and the phase fraction (FCC vs. FCC+BCC or multiphase regions), as determined by techniques such as atom probe tomography, high-resolution TEM, and X-ray diffraction.
generation.mechanism: In the low-Al alloy, high configurational entropy suppresses local chemical clustering despite the inherent attractive interactions, stabilizing a uniform disordered FCC phase. Increasing Al content augments the driving force for local clustering (via strong Al–Ni and Al–Al interactions), overcoming the entropy stabilization and promoting chemical ordering and phase segregation (e.g., formation of dual-phase FCC+BCC regions). This microstructural change is predicted to adversely affect properties that rely on homogeneous dislocation motion and toughening mechanisms.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline low-Al (x = 0.1) alloy, the higher Al content (x = 0.5) alloy will exhibit increased local chemical clustering (evidenced by enhanced Al–Ni and Al–Al pair correlations), a transition from a single-phase FCC to a dual-phase or multiphase microstructure, and concomitantly reduced cryogenic toughness and altered high-temperature strength and environmental resistance. The changes may be on the order of a significant phase fraction shift (e.g., >20% difference in non-FCC phase content) and measurable differences in mechanical property performance.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the low-Al (approximately x = 0.1) Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy, which is known to form a single-phase FCC structure with desirable strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies for alloys within the Al mole fraction range where a transition from entropy-stabilized disorder to clustering-induced ordering is expected (roughly between x ≈ 0.1 and x ≈ 0.5) and under thermal or mechanical conditions (e.g., temperatures below ~600–1000 °C or under high compressive strains) that allow the interplay of pair interactions and configurational entropy to be observed. Outside these composition or condition ranges (e.g., at very high Al content or extreme temperatures), additional mechanisms (such as precipitation kinetics or multiphase segregation due to other elemental interactions) may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical Al mole fraction at which clustering overtakes entropy stabilization may vary with minor differences in processing, and the quantitative relationship between local pair correlation magnitudes and macroscopic property changes is not fully established. Moreover, the relative effects of different external stimuli (temperature, stress, irradiation) on the clustering behavior may introduce complexity.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy specimens with controlled Al mole fractions (e.g., x = 0.1 and x = 0.5) under identical processing conditions to yield homogeneous single-phase samples. Subject both sets to identical isothermal annealing and/or controlled compressive loading (and, optionally, ion irradiation) to promote potential clustering. Use atom probe tomography and high-resolution TEM to quantify local chemical ordering (pair correlations) and phase composition quantitatively. Then, perform mechanical testing at cryogenic and high temperatures to compare property changes.
measurements: Quantitative pair correlation functions (e.g., Al–Al and Al–Ni pair probabilities)
Phase fraction analysis via XRD and TEM mapping
Mechanical properties such as yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and toughness at cryogenic temperatures
Assessment of irradiation-induced precipitation if relevant
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the higher-Al alloy (x = 0.5) does not show a statistically significant increase in local chemical clustering or a measurable shift in phase composition (i.e. remains a single-phase FCC with similar pair correlation functions as the x = 0.1 alloy) and does not exhibit a deterioration in cryogenic toughness or the other targeted properties compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis that enhanced Al-driven local clustering governs phase stability would be falsified.

AbstractIdentifying single phase, high-entropy systems has been a prominent research focus of materials engineering over the past decade. The considerable effort in computational modeling and experimental verification has yielded several methods and descriptors for predicting if a single phase will form; however, the details surrounding the resulting crystal structure have largely remained a mystery. Here, we present a compelling argument for the role of allotropy in determining the crystal structure of a single-phase, high-entropy alloy. High entropy alloys can contain 5 or more elements and must achieve a configurational entropy greater than 1.5R. This study shows that when these high entropy material conditions are met, the majority crystal structure of the non-allotrope forming element plays a dominant role in crystal structure determination. The theory is demonstrated via several approaches, including analysis of 434 unique known single-phase compositions from the literature, thermodynamic modeling of more than 1400 compositions, and experimental synthesis of nine specific alloys that test this hypothesis. The results demonstrate allotropy can identify a subset of compositions

Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. papers.title: Atomistic clustering-ordering and high-strain deformation of an Al0.1CrCoFeNi high-entropy alloy.
papers.approach: Atomistic molecular‐dynamics simulations validated by first‐principles (KKR-CPA) calculations; investigation of pair correlations and response under high-strain compression.
papers.findings: At low Al content, a strong affinity of like pairs (especially dominant Al–Al clustering) is observed at low to moderate temperatures. Under high compressive loading there is a clustering-to-ordering transition not seen under tensile loading, and temperature influences the strength of these correlations.
papers.mechanism: Local chemical clustering driven by strong pair interactions (notably Al–Al and Al–Ni) that compete with configurational entropy; stress and temperature can tip the balance toward short-range ordering.

papers.title: Precipitation behavior of AlxCoCrFeNi high entropy alloys under ion irradiation.
papers.system: AlxCoCrFeNi alloys with varying Al mole fractions
papers.approach: Experimental ion irradiation with structural and compositional characterization (TEM, EDX) to study precipitation evolution under irradiation.
papers.findings: Single-phase HEAs (e.g. with low Al) exhibit high configurational entropy and sluggish atomic diffusion, which suppress the thermodynamic driving force for precipitation even under high-energy displacement events. In contrast, phase-segregated samples indicate sensitivity to local elemental concentrations.
papers.mechanism: High configurational entropy stabilizes the disordered solid solution by offsetting positive mixing enthalpy, while the inherent sluggish diffusion kinetically hinders atomic rearrangements needed for precipitate formation.

papers.title: A first-principles-based high fidelity, high throughput approach for the design of high entropy alloys.
papers.approach: First-principles calculations (KKR-CPA) to map formation energies versus mass density as a function of composition (especially variations in Al and Cr content).
papers.findings: Increased Al content lowers the formation energy and mass density, while variations in Cr content tune the stability of specific lattice types (FCC vs. BCC), suggesting quantitative links between mixing energetics and phase stability.
papers.mechanism: Thermodynamic control through formation enthalpies that balance atomic size, chemical interactions, and entropy; elemental concentrations (especially Al) critically alter the energy landscape governing phase selection.

papers.title: Predictive multiphase evolution in Al-containing high-entropy alloys.
papers.approach: Monte Carlo simulations parameterized with first-principles derived binary interaction parameters to investigate order–disorder transitions and short-range chemical ordering as a function of temperature.
papers.findings: Simulations show temperature-dependent evolution of chemical pair correlations with abrupt changes (e.g., near 600 °C) where ordering (B2-like) and phase separation tendencies become pronounced; specifically, Al shows strong ordering with Co and Ni while Cr and Fe promote chemical clustering at lower temperatures.
papers.mechanism: Temperature modulates the balance between random mixing (favored by configurational entropy) and local chemical ordering driven by strong binary interactions (Al–Co, Al–Ni); this interplay controls whether the single-phase solid solution remains or transforms into ordered/phase-separated microstructures.

papers.title: Mechanical properties and water vapour corrosion behaviour of AlxCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys.
papers.system: AlxCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys with varying Al content
papers.approach: Experimental synthesis (spark plasma sintering) with structural, compositional (XRD, SEM, EDS) and mechanical (tensile, hardness) characterization.
papers.findings: Increasing Al content drives the phase transformation from a single FCC phase at very low Al (x = 0.1) to dual-phase FCC+BCC and eventually to more complex multiphase (including σ phase) microstructures at higher Al levels, significantly affecting mechanical behavior.
papers.mechanism: Elemental segregation driven by the highly negative mixing enthalpy of Al with Ni (and related pairwise interactions) alters the local chemical order and phase stability; thus, Al content directly tunes the balance between disorder (stabilized by configurational entropy) and ordering-induced segregation.

papers.title: The role of allotropy on phase formation in high entropy alloys.
papers.system: General high-entropy alloy systems including Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni variants
papers.approach: Combined analysis of literature data (434 compositions), thermodynamic modeling of >1400 compositions, and targeted experimental synthesis.
papers.findings: The dominant crystal structure of the element that does not exhibit allotropy exerts a significant influence on the resulting phase of the alloy, thereby ruling out certain compositions from forming a single phase and correctly predicting the crystal structure of many HEAs.
papers.mechanism: Allotropy of constituent elements influences phase selection by favoring the crystal structure of the non-allotropic (majority) element, thus affecting the energy balance between configurations. This concept adds to the role of mixing enthalpy and configurational entropy in governing phase stability.

established: Configurational entropy in multiprincipal element systems can stabilize disordered solid solutions despite positive mixing enthalpies.
Al addition, due to its large atomic size and strong pair interactions (particularly with Ni), significantly influences local chemical clustering and subsequent phase transitions.
Sluggish diffusion in high-entropy alloys kinetically restrains phase separation/precipitation under irradiation or high-temperature conditions.
Thermodynamic factors such as formation energy and mixing enthalpies correlate with changes in mass density and lattice type (FCC vs. BCC).

approaches_tried.approach: Atomistic MD simulations combined with first‐principles validation
approaches_tried.outcome: Identified clustering-to-ordering transitions and strong Al–Al correlations that influence phase stability under strain.

approaches_tried.approach: Ion irradiation experiments with microstructural characterization
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated that high configurational entropy and low atomic mobility help maintain single-phase stability by resisting precipitation.
Mapped out formation energies and identified compositional windows where phase stability (FCC vs. BCC) is favored.

approaches_tried.approach: Monte Carlo simulations incorporating first-principles parameters
approaches_tried.outcome: Captured temperature-dependent ordering and phase transitions in Al-containing HEAs, predicting critical ordering temperatures.

mechanisms: Local chemical clustering versus ordering arising from strong binary interactions (e.g., Al–Al, Al–Ni) versus the entropy-driven stabilization of a random solid solution.
Kinetic stabilization by sluggish atomic diffusion that limits phase transformation under irradiation and high-temperature conditions.
Thermodynamic balancing of mixing enthalpy, formation energy, and lattice strain from atomic size mismatches.
Influence of elemental allotropy, where the dominant crystal structure of non-allotropic elements guides the overall phase formation.
disagreements: Some studies note the importance of clustering (with pronounced Al–Al pair correlation) while others emphasize the role of configurational entropy as the primary stabilizer; the relative weight of these effects under different external stimuli (stress, irradiation, temperature) is not fully agreed upon.

Differences exist in predicted ordering transition temperatures (e.g., abrupt changes near 600 °C) between simulation models and experimental observations, suggesting kinetic limitations or additional mechanisms may be involved.
open_questions: To what extent do specific pair correlations (e.g., Al–Al versus Al–Ni) dictate the macroscopic phase stability under various environmental stresses (high temperature, irradiation, cryogenic conditions)?
How do mechanical stress and external stimuli precisely tip the balance between disorder and ordering to yield beneficial phase constituents?
What are the exact boundaries (in terms of composition and temperature) where the stabilizing role of configurational entropy is overcome by local ordering or precipitation phenomena?
How can the influence of elemental allotropy be integrated with mixing enthalpy and entropy considerations to fully predict phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni systems?
opportunities: Conduct controlled comparative studies by systematically varying Al content (e.g., comparing alloys at x = 0.1 versus higher Al contents) while subjecting samples to defined thermal, mechanical, and irradiation environments to directly measure phase evolution.

Combine atomistic simulations (MD, Monte Carlo) with in situ experimental techniques (e.g., TEM under strain, ion irradiation tests) to quantify the interplay between chemical ordering and configurational entropy.
Explore the effects of alloying with elements that modify either the mixing enthalpy or the allotropy characteristics to further tune phase stability and related mechanical properties.

Investigate the role of critical ordering temperatures (e.g., around 600 °C) as a boundary condition, and test observations that would falsify the hypothesis (for example, if altering Al content does not shift the phase stability boundary as predicted).

directions.direction: Test the balance between local chemical clustering driven by strong Al–Ni (and Al–Al) pair interactions versus the stabilizing configurational entropy in determining phase stability.
directions.type: Composition design and mechanistic study (characterization, atomistic simulation, and controlled experiments)
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the suspected core mechanism noted in several studies. It respects constraints regarding temperature, loading, and irradiation by linking local pair correlations with macroscopic phase changes. The underlying physics of strong negative mixing enthalpies (especially for Al–Ni pairs) and the role of configurational entropy are well documented (see PMC4976365, PMC4999872, PMC9279411, and PMC6207727). The study is feasible by comparing alloys of low and modest Al content under controlled annealing and loading conditions, and by using advanced characterization techniques (e.g., atom probe tomography, in situ TEM) to measure local ordering. The observations would be informative for understanding how microstructural evolution governs high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.

directions.direction: Investigate temperature‐driven order–disorder transitions in the alloy using in situ TEM (with compression/tensile) and complementary Monte Carlo simulations to track the clustering‐to‐ordering transition.
directions.type: Processing/heat treatment and in situ characterization
directions.assessment: This study would directly probe the dynamical behavior of the clustering-to-ordering transition under varying temperatures and stress, addressing the mechanism captured by simulations (PMC4976365 and PMC6207727). While it offers insights into transient behavior, its link to the full suite of desired properties (e.g., radiation tolerance) is less direct than a composition–structure relationship. It is feasible but may require correlating with subsequent mechanical tests.

directions.direction: Probe the role of kinetics via sluggish atomic diffusion in stabilizing the single-phase state under irradiation and high-temperature environments.
directions.assessment: This direction builds on the idea that slow diffusion in high entropy alloys kinetically restricts phase separation. It is supported by observations of low atomic mobility (PMC4999872). However, while it explains irradiation and high-temperature stability, it does not as clearly account for the interplay with cryogenic toughness and high-temperature strength driven by local chemical ordering.

directions.direction: Examine the impact of additional alloying (or co-doping with elements that modify mixing enthalpy or promote allotropy match) on phase stability.
directions.assessment: Adjusting the alloy by adding minor elements (or altering the Al content further) could shed light on how changes in interatomic interactions affect phase stability. Although promising, this direction adds a variable (extra elemental effects) that may complicate the controlled analysis of the intrinsic Al-driven mechanism and its direct relevance to the target properties.

directions.direction: Integrate high-throughput first-principles and Monte Carlo modeling with targeted experiments under varied thermal and mechanical loading to simulate multiphase evolution.
directions.assessment: This approach would robustly link computational predictions (PMC6207727, PMC9279411) with experimental observables. While comprehensive, it involves complex cross-scale integration which may dilute the focus on a single mechanistic hypothesis governing phase stability relevant to the target property mix.

choice.direction: Test the balance between local chemical clustering driven by strong Al–Ni (and Al–Al) pair interactions versus configurational entropy in determining phase stability.
choice.why: This direction most directly addresses the central limitation by proposing a single mechanistic hypothesis: that local chemical interactions (especially those involving Al) control the onset of short-range clustering which competes with the entropy‐stabilized disordered solid solution. This mechanism is linked to observed changes in phase constitution (FCC, FCC+BCC, or multiphase states) that in turn correlate with high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness. The concept is supported by multiple pieces of evidence (e.g., PMC4976365, PMC4999872, and PMC9279411) and is feasible to test by systematically varying Al content and subjecting specimens to controlled thermal and mechanical conditions.
